strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: using in-the-wild YouTube house-tour videos to enable camera-parameter-free 3D indoor semantic occupancy pre-training, directly addressing the well-known scarcity of annotated indoor 3D data and the difficulty of acquiring camera intrinsics/extrinsics.

Fully automated and scalable data pipeline that combines clip splitting, outdoor-scene filtering, Dust3R-based camera/point-cloud estimation, VFM semantic labeling, and voxelization, with practical post-processing heuristics (radius/statistical filtering, z-up alignment, metric scaling) that make the pipeline usable at scale.

Consistent positive empirical results across two benchmarks and many annotation regimes; the annotation-efficient gains (e.g., +5.25 mIoU at 10% NYUv2, +4.45 mIoU at 10% OccScanNet) are the most convincing evidence and demonstrate genuine practical value of the pre-training paradigm.
The pre-training paradigm is model-agnostic and requires only minimal architectural modification (the feature dimension D), which makes the approach broadly applicable and easy to adopt.
The paper is generally well-organized, the pipeline is clearly described, and the qualitative visualizations (Figs. 3–4) usefully complement the quantitative results.
weaknesses: Claim–evidence mismatch: the abstract states the method achieves "state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on two popular benchmarks," yet the reported zero-shot numbers (9.95% mIoU / 19.41% IoU on NYUv2, 4.61% mIoU / 9.30% IoU on OccScanNet) are essentially near-random and do not substantiate any meaningful zero-shot capability. This overstatement should be corrected.

Full-annotation gains are marginal (+1.04 mIoU on NYUv2, +0.30 mIoU on OccScanNet) and, as the checklist itself admits, no error bars or statistical-significance tests are reported. Without variance estimates it is unclear whether these improvements exceed run-to-run noise, which weakens the "state-of-the-art" framing.

For a paper whose primary contribution is a dataset/pipeline (YouTube-Occ), the dataset will not be released publicly. This substantially limits the community value of the contribution and undermines reproducibility of the data-driven claims.

No component ablations are provided. The specific roles of the VFM-based superpixel grouping, the contrastive distillation loss, the choice of DINOv2/SAN, the use of supervoxel majority voting, and the use of YouTube-Occ data versus self-training on the target dataset are all unexamined, so the source of the reported gains is unclear.

The pipeline depends entirely on off-the-shelf models (Dust3R, SAN, DINOv2), but there is no analysis of the quality/noise of the resulting pseudo-labels or of how reconstruction and segmentation errors propagate into the occupancy supervision. This is a critical omission given that label noise from these models could plausibly explain both the small full-data gains and the near-random zero-shot numbers.

Apparent inconsistencies between tables and figures are not explained: e.g., NYUv2 10% is 21.64 mIoU in Table 3 but 22.68 mIoU in Fig. 5, and OccScanNet 10% is 36.40 mIoU in Table 4 but 42.91 mIoU in Fig. 5. The experimental setup distinguishing these numbers (cross-dataset pre-training vs. in-domain pre-training) needs to be clarified to avoid confusion about what is being compared.

The pre-training claim is only compared against random initialization. Other self-supervised 3D representation-learning methods discussed in related work (e.g., CrossPoint, MM-Point, or other web-data pipelines) are not used as baselines, so the advantage of the proposed distillation over existing alternatives is not established.

The "first work to explore in-the-wild videos for semantic occupancy prediction" claim is arguable given prior web-data and YouTube-based learning works (e.g., YouTube-VLN, web-data pipelines for other tasks), and the novelty of the contrastive distillation component relative to prior 2D-to-3D distillation work is not sharply delineated.

Dataset scale is modest (14,592 frames from 651 clips), and there is little analysis of the domain gap between YouTube real-estate footage and the target benchmarks, nor of the implications of using residential videos scraped from the Internet (privacy/ethics are mentioned only cursorily).

strengths: Introduces a novel and practical data source for indoor 3D semantic occupancy: real-estate house-tour videos on YouTube, avoiding the high cost of manual 3D annotation and household privacy concerns associated with existing benchmarks.

Proposes a fully automated, scalable pipeline (video splitting, outdoor filtering, Dust3R-based camera/depth/point cloud reconstruction, VFM-based semantic labeling, and voxelization) that removes the need for pre-configured intrinsics/extrinsics, which is a meaningful step toward learning 3D priors from in-the-wild data.

The proposed VFM-assisted superpixel-supervoxel contrastive distillation is conceptually clean, model-agnostic (only feature dimension changes between pre-training and fine-tuning), and aligns object-level 2D region knowledge with 3D occupancy features.

Reports consistent gains on both NYUv2 and OccScanNet, and the annotation-efficiency study (Fig. 5, Tables 3-4) shows the pre-training is especially beneficial in low-label regimes (e.g., +5.25 mIoU at 10% NYUv2 labels), which is the most compelling evidence for the method's value.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear pipeline and qualitative figures, and the checklist appropriately discloses several limitations.
weaknesses: The dataset, which is a headline contribution (YouTube-Occ), is explicitly stated to 'not be released in public' (Sec. 6). For a paper whose primary novelty is a data source, this severely limits reproducibility, verifiability, and community impact, and weakens the dataset contribution considerably.

Gains under full supervision are marginal: +1.04 mIoU on NYUv2 and +0.30 mIoU on OccScanNet. Given that the pre-training requires substantial additional compute (a separate 30-epoch pre-training stage plus 30-epoch fine-tuning on 4x A6000), the practical value at high label budgets is modest and should be discussed more honestly.

The abstract and introduction claim 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on two popular benchmarks,' but the zero-shot results in Table 5 are very weak (9.95% mIoU on NYUv2, 4.61% mIoU on OccScanNet). Characterizing this as 'state-of-the-art zero-shot' is misleading relative to how the term is normally understood and should be reworded.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported (as acknowledged in the checklist), despite several claimed improvements being on the order of 0.3-1.0 mIoU, which is within typical run-to-run variance.

The ablation is thin: the contribution of individual components (superpixel vs. pixel-level distillation, choice of VFM (SAN), choice of 2D embedding network (DINOv2), temperature, etc.) is not isolated, so it is unclear what drives the improvements.

The method relies on off-the-shelf Dust3R for pose/intrinsic/depth estimation and SAN for semantic labeling, but there is no analysis of how errors in these components propagate to the distilled 3D representations, nor any quantitative measure of reconstruction/label quality of YouTube-Occ.

The term 'self-supervised' is used loosely: the pre-training depends on DINOv2 features and the SAN VFM, both of which are trained with supervision. The method is better described as cross-modal distillation than as self-supervised learning.

The pipeline's dependence on Dust3R means the 'without pre-known camera parameters' claim is achieved only by delegating camera estimation to another learned model; the practical robustness of this on noisy YouTube footage (motion blur, dynamic objects, rolling shutter) is not analyzed.
The size of YouTube-Occ (14,592 frames, 651 clips) is relatively small for a pre-training corpus, and no analysis is provided on how performance scales with pre-training data size.

Semantic voxelization uses a majority-vote of point labels, but no details are given on how ambiguity/unknown classes or noisy point clouds affect the supervision quality of the resulting occupancy grids.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and practical problem: reducing the reliance on expensive, privacy-sensitive indoor 3D scanning by exploiting in-the-wild web video, which is a reasonable direction for scalable 3D pre-training.

Provides an end-to-end automated pipeline (video curation, clip splitting, Dust3R-based reconstruction, semantic labeling, voxelization) for turning YouTube house-tour footage into occupancy-style training data, with non-trivial engineering effort (14,592 frames / 651 clips).

The superpixel-supervoxel contrastive distillation objective is simple, model-agnostic, and conceptually sensible for injecting 2D vision-foundation-model region knowledge into a 3D occupancy network.
Experiments cover two benchmarks (NYUv2, OccScanNet) and include an annotation-efficiency study across multiple label percentages, which is a useful evaluation angle.
weaknesses: Reported gains over the strongest baseline (Symphonies) are marginal and plausibly within noise: +1.04% mIoU / +1.21% IoU on NYUv2 (30.74 vs 29.70) and +0.30% mIoU / +0.25% IoU on OccScanNet (58.15 vs 57.85). No error bars, variance, or significance tests are reported (the checklist itself answers 'No' for statistical significance), so the central performance claim is not convincingly supported.

The abstract/contribution claims 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on two popular benchmarks,' but the actual zero-shot numbers are 9.95% mIoU / 19.41% IoU (NYUv2) and 4.61% mIoU / 9.30% IoU (OccScanNet) — essentially non-functional. Presenting this as a headline 'SOTA' result is misleading and does not reflect the true capability of the method.

A core stated contribution is the YouTube-Occ dataset, yet the paper explicitly states it 'will not be released in public.' This removes the primary artifact that would let others reproduce or build on the work, and materially weakens both the dataset contribution and reproducibility.

The pipeline depends entirely on off-the-shelf models (Dust3R for reconstruction/pose, SAN for segmentation, DINOv2 for features), and the quality/robustness of the derived geometry and labels on handheld YouTube footage is never validated. Errors in reconstruction or semantic labeling would silently corrupt the voxel targets, yet no analysis of pipeline fidelity is provided.

No ablation isolates the proposed contrastive superpixel-supervoxel distillation from simpler alternatives (e.g., per-pixel/per-voxel distillation, or no distillation), and the only comparison is against random initialization. It is therefore unclear whether the small gains come from the proposed loss or simply from seeing more (unlabeled) data.

Numerical inconsistencies across the paper raise reliability concerns: e.g., NYUv2 100%-label mIoU is 30.74 in Table 1/Figure 5(a) but 30.64 in Table 3; the 'Ours' entries differ between tables for the same nominal setting.

Limited methodological novelty: distilling 2D foundation features into 3D representations is well established, and the region-grouping variant is incremental. Related self-supervised 3D methods (CrossPoint, MM-Point) are discussed but never compared against.

The claim of operating 'without the need for any pre-knowledge of intrinsic or extrinsic camera parameters' is overstated, since camera parameters are in fact obtained via Dust3R; the method relies on strong learned priors rather than avoiding camera knowledge.

The checklist responses are partly inconsistent with the paper (e.g., affirming SOTA/broader-impact claims that the evidence does not substantiate, and stating the dataset is not released while listing it as a contribution), and limitations are acknowledged only superficially (dynamic-object handling left entirely to future work).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated problem: the scarcity and privacy concerns of annotated indoor 3D semantic occupancy data. Framing the solution as learning from abundant, uncalibrated in-the-wild YouTube videos is a compelling and novel angle, and the authors are (to their knowledge) the first to apply web-data learning to 3D semantic occupancy prediction.

The proposed data curation pipeline is thoughtfully constructed and technically sound: real-estate footage selection for stable camera motion and static content, outdoor filtering with a Places classifier, Dust3R for joint camera/pose/point-cloud estimation, SAN for open-vocabulary segmentation, and a heuristic scale normalization (2.8 m wall height) to obtain a canonical metric space. The pipeline is largely automatic and scalable.

The empirical analysis in Table 1 (naive zero-shot / joint training with pseudo-labels performs at or below the raw pseudo-label quality) is a valuable negative result that motivates the distillation framework. The diagnosis of geometric scale misalignment and semantic misalignment is well-reasoned and adds scientific value beyond the specific method.

The pre-training framework is model-agnostic and evaluated on three architecturally diverse backbones (MonoScene, Symphonies, EmbodiedOcc) across two benchmarks (NYUv2, Occ-ScanNet), with consistent gains. This is a more thorough evaluation than many single-backbone papers, and the few-shot results (+3.29% mIoU at 5% on NYUv2, +2.36% at 10% on Occ-ScanNet) demonstrate meaningful data-efficiency benefits.

Ablations (Tables 5 and 6) convincingly show the complementarity of the region and prototype losses, and justify the design choices (Gaussian rendering vs. direct projection; momentum/prototype configuration). The comparison against alternative strategies (HASSCC, GaussRender, Pri3D) in Table 4 helps situate the method.
The paper is generally clear and well-organized, and limitations are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The absolute improvements are modest: +1.95% mIoU on NYUv2 and +1.67% mIoU on Occ-ScanNet for Symphonies. While consistent across backbones, these margins are small relative to the noise typically seen on such benchmarks, and the 'state-of-the-art' claim depends on baselines that are not all directly comparable (e.g., EmbodiedOcc++, RoboOcc). The practical significance of the contribution hinges largely on the few-shot gains, which are more convincing.

Methodological details are sparse in several places. The temperatures τ_region and τ_proto are never specified; the pre-training schedule, number of pre-training iterations/epochs, and any loss weighting between L_region and L_proto (the total is simply stated as the sum) are not fully given. This hampers reproducibility and makes it hard to judge the sensitivity of the framework.

The 2.8-meter wall-height assumption used for metric scale normalization is a strong and largely unvalidated heuristic. No ablation or sensitivity analysis is provided on this value, yet it directly affects voxelization and the geometric pseudo-labels. This is a substantive methodological gap given that scale misalignment is identified as a core problem.

The reconstruction quality of Dust3R on uncalibrated in-the-wild video is never quantitatively evaluated. Since the entire pipeline depends on the geometry, the absence of any geometric accuracy metric (e.g., against held-out known geometry) leaves an important part of the contribution unverified. Similarly, there is no analysis of how many downloaded videos/clips are discarded by the filtering stages, or of the final dataset's actual scene diversity.

The individual technical components—region-level contrastive distillation against DINOv2 features and prototype-based cross-scene contrastive learning—are largely adaptations of existing ideas (e.g., GaussTR, AGO, AutoOcc). Novelty resides mainly in the pipeline combination rather than in new algorithmic machinery, which slightly weakens the algorithmic contribution.

Data reproducibility is a concern: the dataset is built from YouTube real-estate videos that may be removed or made private, and redistribution of raw videos/frames may raise licensing issues. The paper does not discuss how it will handle this, despite promising to release code and data.

The paper does not clearly separate gains attributable to the data pipeline versus those from the distillation losses; the zero-shot/joint-training results already show the pseudo-labels are weak, so it would be informative to know how much the pipeline design (e.g., scale normalization, filtering) versus the losses contributes to the final gains.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck in indoor 3D semantic occupancy prediction—the scarcity of large-scale annotated 3D data due to privacy concerns and costly scanning equipment—by proposing a data-centric solution that leverages uncalibrated in-the-wild internet videos, which is a compelling and underexplored direction.

Introduces a complete and reasonably well-described automated data curation pipeline (video collection/filtering, point cloud reconstruction via Dust3R, open-vocabulary segmentation via SAN, and occupancy voxelization), demonstrating that a rich pre-training corpus (YouTube-Occ, 100K+ frames across 5,241 scenes) can be constructed without any manual annotation.

Provides a thoughtful empirical analysis showing that naive supervision with pseudo-labels fails (Sec. 5.2, Tab. 1), and uses this negative result to motivate the proposed pre-training framework—this is a scientifically honest and instructive finding.

The dual-alignment pre-training framework (intra-frame voxel-anchored Gaussianization with region contrastive loss + cross-scene class-prototype contrastive loss) is clearly motivated, technically coherent, and validated through ablations (Tab. 5 and Tab. 6).

Demonstrates model-agnostic applicability by validating across three distinct architectures (MonoScene, Symphonies, EmbodiedOcc) and two benchmarks (NYUv2, Occ-ScanNet), achieving consistent improvements and SOTA results (31.65% mIoU on NYUv2, 49.38% mIoU on Occ-ScanNet).

The few-shot evaluations (Tab. 3) show substantial gains under limited supervision (e.g., +3.29% mIoU at 5% labels and +5.09% at 10% on NYUv2), which is a practically valuable result and supports the claim of improved data efficiency.

Includes reasonable ablations (projection variants, prototype momentum, semantic threshold) and qualitative visualizations (Figs. 4 and 5) that help substantiate the design choices and observed improvements.

Writing is generally clear, the pipeline figure (Fig. 2) and framework figure (Fig. 3) are informative, and the paper acknowledges limitations in the conclusion (invisible/occluded voxels, wall-height assumption, extension to multi-view/temporal networks).
weaknesses: The technical contribution is heavily dependent on off-the-shelf foundation models (Dust3R for geometry, SAN for segmentation, DINOv2 for features), so the core novelty lies primarily in the pipeline orchestration and the distillation losses rather than in new modeling or representation learning; the marginal contribution over existing components could be more clearly delineated.

The absolute performance gains on the full datasets are modest (+1.95% mIoU on NYUv2, +1.67% on Occ-ScanNet), and while the authors claim SOTA, the improvement margins over strong baselines are small; a more careful discussion of whether these gains are within run-to-run variance would strengthen the claims.

The metric-scale recovery relies on a crude 2.8-meter wall-height assumption, which is a strong and potentially fragile prior; its impact on scenes with atypical ceiling heights (e.g., vaulted rooms, basements) is not analyzed, and this may limit generalization to broader indoor environments.

The video source is restricted to real estate footage with specific assumptions (smooth camera motion, mostly static content, indoor); the paper does not adequately discuss how the pipeline would behave on more dynamic, hand-held, or non-real-estate indoor videos, which weakens the generalizability claims of the 'in-the-wild' framing.

Despite privacy being cited as a primary motivation for avoiding indoor scanning, collecting and processing in-home YouTube videos raises its own privacy and legal/ethical considerations (e.g., identifiable personal spaces, terms of service, consent) that are not discussed; a societal-impact discussion is largely absent.

The paper does not provide a detailed failure analysis of the pseudo-label quality (Fig. 4 shows visible discrepancies from GT), nor does it quantify the downstream effect of individual pseudo-label error sources (scale vs. semantic misalignment), making it harder to understand the ceiling of the proposed approach.

Comparison against alternative strategies is limited to a few auxiliary-loss and pre-training baselines (HASSAC, GaussRender, Pri3D); comparisons with other web-data or self-supervised 3D pre-training methods, and with any data-augmentation or synthetic-data baselines, would better situate the contribution.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: the dataset and code are promised upon release, but key pipeline details (e.g., heuristic filters, post-processing for scale ambiguity, exact clip-splitting criteria) are described at a high level and would benefit from more precise specification.

The framework assumes the 2D and 3D feature spaces can be aligned via masked average pooling and contrastive losses, but the paper does not analyze how sensitive the method is to the quality of the open-vocabulary segmentation (SAN) masks, which are central to both the pseudo-labels and the alignment targets.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely bottleneck in indoor 3D semantic occupancy: the scarcity of large-scale, annotated 3D data, and proposes a data-centric web-video alternative to manual annotation.

The automated curation pipeline is a substantial engineering effort, sensibly composing 3D foundation models (Dust3R for geometry) and 2D foundation models (SAN for open-vocabulary segmentation, DINOv2 for features) to produce geometric and semantic pseudo-labels at scale.

The pre-training framework is deliberately model-agnostic and is evaluated across three distinct architectures (MonoScene, Symphonies, EmbodiedOcc) on two benchmarks (NYUv2, Occ-ScanNet), which lends some credibility to the generality of the reported gains.

The empirical finding that naive direct supervision with pseudo-labels is harmful (Table 1, zero-shot 8.41% mIoU) is a useful negative result that motivates the distillation formulation and is honestly reported.
The few-shot experiments (Table 3) show the most convincing evidence, with gains of roughly +3 to +5% mIoU at 5-10% labeled data, supporting the claim that web data can improve data efficiency.
The ablation studies (Tables 5 and 6) reasonably isolate the contributions of the region loss, prototype loss, Gaussianization, and prototype momentum, and the paper explicitly discusses limitations.
weaknesses: The headline full-dataset gains are marginal (about +1.95% mIoU on NYUv2 and +1.67% on Occ-ScanNet) and are reported without error bars, multiple seeds, or any statistical significance testing, so it is unclear whether the improvements exceed run-to-run variance. This weakens the central claim of 'consistent gains'.

The technical novelty is incremental. Voxel-anchored Gaussianization is essentially standard differentiable Gaussian rendering applied to voxel features, and class-prototype contrastive distillation is a well-established technique; the paper largely transfers these to occupancy rather than introducing fundamentally new machinery.

The pipeline relies on crude geometric heuristics, notably the hard-coded 2.8-meter wall-height assumption to recover metric scale from uncalibrated monocular video. The authors themselves identify scale ambiguity as an ill-posed problem, yet this systematic bias directly affects the quality of the occupancy pseudo-labels and is not quantitatively analyzed.

The data source is narrow: only real-estate footage (predominantly houses with smooth camera motion) is used, which contradicts the abstract's claim of 'diverse and rich' data and raises concerns about domain bias relative to the broader range of indoor scenes the benchmarks target.

Evaluation fairness is unclear. Tables mix reproduced results (marked with †) and original numbers from prior work, and the pre-training rows are stacked on top of reproduced baselines; without consistent re-training of all competing methods, the reported comparisons may not be apples-to-apples.

Reproducibility is limited: code and data are only promised, not released, and the pipeline depends on many external foundation models (Dust3R, SAN, DINOv2) and unspecified preprocessing details, making faithful reproduction difficult.

Key dataset-construction details are underspecified, e.g., how the 100,372 frames across 5,241 scenes were selected and filtered, how duplicates/near-duplicate clips are handled, and how the class taxonomy is mapped from open-vocabulary segmentation to the 11 benchmark classes.

The 'first to use unlabeled, uncalibrated in-the-wild videos for 3D semantic occupancy' claim is strong and not rigorously substantiated against the growing body of web-data 3D perception work, and the paper provides no dedicated discussion of the legal/privacy implications of scraping and redistributing web video for training.

Given the complexity of the multi-model pipeline and pre-training framework, the cost-benefit tradeoff relative to the small full-data gains is not discussed, and there is no comparison against simpler alternatives such as additional in-domain data or other pseudo-label refinement strategies.
